title: The Mango Thief (Português)
summary: Two men claim ownership of a sweet mango tree laden with ripe fruit. Birbal uses a Solomon-like test to determine the authentic planter. [PT]
full_text:
In a fertile village bordering the river Yamuna, an ancient and extraordinarily sweet mango tree stood near a boundary hedge. That summer, the tree was bowed low with hundreds of golden, fragrant Dussehri mangoes. Two neighboring farmers, Ramlal and Shyamlal, appeared before Emperor Akbar's imperial court, violently shouting and accusing each other.

Ramlal wept: 'Sire! Twelve years ago, I planted the sapling, carried water from the river every morning, fenced it from wild deer, and fertilized the soil! Now that it bears heavenly fruit, Shyamlal claims it grew on his side of the hedge!'

Shyamlal yelled back: 'Lies, Your Majesty! The roots spring from my land! Ramlal is an envious scoundrel who wishes to rob my harvest!'

There were no written land records for the village border, and the village panchayat was evenly divided, half supporting Ramlal and half supporting Shyamlal.

Akbar turned the case over to Birbal. 'How will you uncover who planted the tree twelve years ago?'

Birbal listened to both men, stroked his beard, and said in a grave voice: 'Since the boundary is uncertain and the testimony is deadlocked, neither of you can be granted the tree. The imperial court shall settle this fairly: guards, take axes to the orchard! Chop the mango tree down the middle! Cut the trunk into two equal halves of timber for each man, and divide the plucked mangoes into two equal baskets!'

Shyamlal immediately nodded with enthusiasm: 'A wise and fair judgment! If I cannot have the whole tree, neither shall he! Cut it down at once, Sire!'

Hearing this, Ramlal fell face-down upon the marble floor, weeping piteously:

'No, Emperor! I beg of you, do not chop down the tree! I watered it for twelve long years; it is like my own child! Give the tree and all its sweet mangoes to Shyamlal! Let him have everything, but spare the life of the tree!'

Birbal stepped down from the dais, helped Ramlal to his feet, and addressed Emperor Akbar:

'Your Majesty, the judgment is clear. A thief and an imposter is eager to destroy what he never labored to create, for he cares only for selfish spite. But the true father who nurtured the tree with his sweat would rather surrender his claim than see the living tree slain.'

Akbar awarded the entire orchard to Ramlal, ordered Shyamlal heavily fined and sentenced to prison, and praised Birbal's profound understanding of human devotion.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
